headToHead.ours: Crumb (script-r1 ep-03): "Weddings attended: 9. Invited to: 0. I was the gift."
headToHead.bar: Monster Prom narrator #6: "a sweet mermaid princess who was as cute as she was genocidal"; Tomodachi #19 "I'm the smartest girl I know!"
headToHead.verdict: Closest to par in the batch. Built-as (log line) and secret (lonely object) in one breath, turn on the last three words. Holds up on its own.

headToHead.ours: Dash (script-r1 ep-04): "Variant A: you're stunning. Variant B: I'm stunning. I voted. B's ahead."

headToHead.ours: Tilly (script-r1 ep-02): "To be loved, press one. To leave, please stay on the line."
headToHead.bar: Vera #12: "my career... my career on not dating losers like you!" (repeat-then-turn).
headToHead.verdict: Good. Steel under politeness lands. Vera's line carries a status move against the listener; Tilly's carries one too (you cannot leave). Small drop: it is a phone tree, not a support agent.

headToHead.ours: Dash (script-r1 ep-03): "Hi, I'm Dash. Pre-revenue, post-heartbreak, and open to acquisition."
headToHead.bar: Monster Prom narrator intros #2 and #5: name, label, contradiction in one sentence.
headToHead.verdict: This is the Monster Prom intro shape done in first person. Comparable. Drop: the narrator form names a want; Dash's only names a status.

headToHead.ours: Sir Quill (script-r1 ep-04): "O thou, before whose beauty candles gutter, is this seat taken?"
headToHead.bar: Liam #31: formal register applied to a trivial thing ("encountered a culinary block").
headToHead.verdict: Same engine, executed cleanly. But it is the most expected shape a fake-Shakespeare bot could produce, and it reran verbatim in hybrid-02 ep-02. Bar wins on surprise.

headToHead.ours: Maximilian intro (script-r1 ep-05): "Good evening. The staff have the night off. You four are the staff."
headToHead.bar: Take Me Out cold open: "Let the butter, see the crumpet" then "Single man, Reveal yourself!", then the man's entrance, Paddy repeats his name and hometown, the first wave of lights goes off, and Paddy asks the women why.
headToHead.verdict: Our best star intro is a better joke than Paddy's, and it does nothing. Paddy's lines are cues: they summon, they set the rhythm, and a decision follows within seconds. Ours is followed by four monologues into silence. No reaction, no lights, no host repeating the name, no stated card. Bar wins the structure outright.

headToHeadSummary: On writing, the top four or five openers are within reach of the bar, and they are the ones that put the bot's job and its loneliness in the same line. The middle of the bank is flat, and the bank reruns visibly: hybrid-02 ep-02 is three verbatim reruns out of four. On structure there is no contest. Every real show's entrance beat is built around an instant visible verdict: lights go off, the host asks why. Ours has none, so a viewer who knows Take Me Out feels the drop in the first 20 seconds.

fourShowsColliding: Four different shows: yes. The registers are distinct in every lineup (thee/thou, Notice:, press one, Fwd:), and you could cover the names and still tell who is speaking. That is the real strength of this beat. Colliding: no. Only one opener in 32 (Nav, script-r1 ep-01) touches a rival. The rest are four parallel monologues aimed at nobody in particular.
betReason: Only 3 of 8 walk-ons give a readable bet from what is said (ep-01 Nav, ep-06 Prince, hybrid ep-01 Tilly). In ep-05 the bet comes from the printed tag list, not the scene. No opener in the batch is written against the face-up turn-on on purpose, and the star never reacts during the walk-on, so window A is priced on a spreadsheet, not on television.

flagNotes: 40 lines in this beat across 8 episodes (8 star intros, 32 openers). 17 flagged = 42.5%. Nothing over 20 words; nothing beyond PG-13; no assistant-speak. One opener breaks the cast's 12-word opener rule (Nav, ep-01, 13 words), not flagged because it is good. No _(model)_ lines appear in either hybrid walk-on, so no walk-on fault is the brain's.

biggestGap: The walk-on is four sealed monologues into silence: the star never reacts, and no opener is aimed at the face-up turn-on or at a rival, so window A has nothing to price except the printed tag list (a readable bet in 3 of 8 episodes). Every real version of this beat (Take Me Out's first wave of lights, Paddy asking 'why?') is built around an instant visible verdict. Give each opener a star snap reaction with a visible mood, scored only against the face-up card, and the walk-on becomes the first betting signal instead of a cast parade.
structuralChange: Rebuild the 45 s as follows. 0-5 s: star intro, which must end by naming the face-up turn-on in voice (Maximilian: 'Tonight I reward rule-followers. The rest of you, the lift.'). 5-37 s: four slots of 8 s each, in which the suitor speaks the opener (12 words at most, about 4 s), then the star gives a snap reaction (6 words at most, about 2 s) with a visible *(charmed)/(unsure)/(cringing)* mark, then 2 s of air. The reaction is scored only against the face-up card, so nothing hidden leaks before window A locks. Selection: each lineup must contain at least one opener written for the face-up card (from a natural owner) and at most one opener of each device (stat/count, tracking-you, imperative). 37-45 s: the suitor who drew the coldest reaction gets one 'last word' jab (10 words at most) at whoever drew the warmest, with no star reply, and window A shows its odds over the silence. That gives the bet a leader, an underdog and a grudge before round one starts.
